concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: Research only checkpoint mechanisms, modes, scheduling, failure conditions, diagnostics, and documented evolution.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpoint scheduling
concepts.reason: Thresholds and callback configuration determine when checkpoints execute.

concepts.name: Reader-limited checkpoint progress
concepts.reason: Reader end marks constrain safe transfer and checkpoint completion.

concepts.name: Checkpoint synchronization ordering
concepts.reason: Storage synchronization ordering protects checkpointed data against corruption.

concepts.name: WAL recycling and truncation
concepts.reason: Recycling and truncation have distinct conditions and file-size consequences.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE
concepts.reason: PASSIVE defines checkpoint progress without waiting for readers or writers.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL
concepts.reason: FULL adds explicit waiting conditions and writer exclusion.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART
concepts.reason: RESTART adds the reader condition needed for subsequent WAL reuse.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE
concepts.reason: TRUNCATE adds physical log truncation on successful completion.

concepts.name: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP
concepts.reason: NOOP exposes checkpoint status without checkpointing frames.

concepts.name: Checkpoint lock contention and fallback
concepts.reason: Lock contention and busy-handler termination qualify completion guarantees.

concepts.name: Checkpoint status and database selection
concepts.reason: Output counters and database-selection rules determine how callers interpret results.

concepts.name: Large-transaction checkpoint limits
concepts.reason: Transaction boundaries and documented version changes explain checkpoint-related WAL growth.

concepts.name: WAL read-path indexing
concepts.reason: General reader page lookup and shared-memory indexing extend beyond checkpoint progress tracking.

concepts.name: Rollback journaling
concepts.reason: Rollback journaling is a separate transaction mechanism rather than a checkpoint subcomponent.

concepts.name: WAL mode activation
concepts.reason: Journal-mode conversion and VFS eligibility are configuration topics outside checkpoint depth.

claims.text: A checkpoint moves WAL transactions back into the original database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: Every new database connection enables automatic checkpointing with a default threshold of 1000 pages or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT setting.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: Automatic checkpoints and checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.

claims.text: A checkpoint must stop at a WAL page past the end mark of any current reader.
claims.quote: the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage before its content is moved into the database.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database

claims.text: The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.
claims.quote: and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL. Checkpoint also requires more seeking.

claims.text: Checkpointing normally does not truncate the WAL file; S1 identifies journal_size_limit as an exception.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set).

claims.text: The thread performing the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit runs the automatic checkpoint by default.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: The reader end-mark limit prevents the checkpoint from overwriting database content that an active reader uses.
claims.quote: The checkpoint has to stop at that point because otherwise it might overwrite part of the database file that the reader is actively using.

claims.text: The checkpoint records progress in the wal-index and resumes from that position on its next invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: Continuously overlapping active readers can prevent checkpoint completion and cause unbounded WAL growth.
claims.quote: if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers to finish.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL invokes the busy handler while waiting for no database writer and for all readers to use the most recent snapshot.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: A pending SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL blocks new writers while allowing new readers to proceed unimpeded.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART adds a post-checkpoint wait until all readers read only from the database file.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL with the addition that after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE extends SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART by truncating the log to zero bytes just before a successful return.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP checkpoints zero frames and is used to obtain pnLog and pnCkpt values.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: Passing N less than or equal to zero to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint disables automatic checkpoints entirely.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers checkpointing after a transaction commits when the WAL contains at least N frames.
claims.quote: causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: If another process is checkpointing, failure to obtain the exclusive checkpoint lock returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned.

claims.text: Checkpoint-lock contention does not invoke a configured busy handler.
claims.quote: the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: If the busy handler returns zero while acquiring the writer lock or waiting for readers, the checkpoint falls back to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE behavior.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: The busy-handler termination fallback returns SQLITE_BUSY even though it attempts further nonblocking checkpoint work.
claims.quote: checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: pnCkpt counts all checkpointed frames in the log, including frames checkpointed before the current call.
claims.quote: *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: Successful SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE sets both pnLog and pnCkpt to zero.
claims.quote: upon successful completion of an SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE, the log file will have been truncated to zero bytes and so both *pnLog and *pnCkpt will be set to zero.

claims.text: Configuring sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint replaces an existing sqlite3_wal_hook callback.
claims.quote: The callback registered by this function replaces any existing callback registered using sqlite3_wal_hook() .

claims.text: Registering a sqlite3_wal_hook callback disables automatic checkpointing configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint.
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync operation.
claims.quote: with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation (fsync() on unix or FlushFileBuffers() on windows).

claims.text: As of SQLite 3.11.0, dated 2016-02-15, the WAL for a single transaction should be proportional in size to that transaction.
claims.quote: As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), the WAL file for a single transaction should be proportional in size to the transaction itself.

claims.text: Before SQLite 3.11.0, transactions exceeding the page cache could write the same page into the WAL multiple times.
claims.quote: However, with older versions of SQLite, the same page might be written into the WAL file multiple times if the transaction grows larger than the page cache.

claims.text: The WAL cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.

claims.text: Attempting checkpoints during reader gaps can avoid checkpoint starvation.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: Selecting an attached database that is not in WAL mode returns SQLITE_OK with both output counters set to -1.
claims.quote: If database zDb is the name of an attached database that is not in WAL mode, SQLITE_OK is returned and both *pnLog and *pnCkpt set to -1.

claims.text: When zDb is NULL or empty, the operation targets all attached WAL databases and the output counters are undefined.
claims.quote: the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.

claims.text: During an operation across attached WAL databases, SQLITE_BUSY does not stop processing remaining databases and is returned at the end.
claims.quote: If an SQLITE_BUSY error is encountered when processing one or more of the attached WAL databases, the operation is still attempted on any remaining attached databases and SQLITE_BUSY is returned at the end.

claims.text: During an operation across attached databases, an error other than SQLITE_BUSY stops processing immediately.
claims.quote: If any other error occurs while processing an attached database, processing is abandoned and the error code is returned to the caller immediately.

limitations: Only the frozen S1–S3 excerpts were used. No tools, external sources, agents, installations, or persistent changes were used.
Rates equal new atomic claims divided by cumulative claims after each pass. Pass 3 added 19.44%; two consecutive passes below 5% did not occur.
All six deepening questions were considered: mechanism, boundaries, exceptions, disagreement, primary-source wording, and historical change. Unsupported answers were not counted as claims.
The packet supplies no independent expert disagreement or competing interpretation. Documentation tensions cannot establish an expert controversy.
S1 says RESTART and TRUNCATE may block readers, while S2 says RESTART does not impede readers. Their precise reconciliation is unsupported by these excerpts.

S1 describes manual RESTART and TRUNCATE as ensuring completion; S2 qualifies that wording with busy-handler termination, PASSIVE fallback, and SQLITE_BUSY. Unconditional completion is therefore not asserted.

S1's application-initiated section lists three modes and later says RESET; S2 explicitly documents PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART, TRUNCATE, and NOOP. The packet does not establish when or why this documentation mismatch arose.
Historical evidence is limited to the SQLite 3.11.0 large-transaction WAL-size change. Origins of checkpoint modes and changes in expert understanding are unsupported.

The hard three-pass and 36-claim budgets prevent exhaustive coverage. At least one further pass appears useful for writer-lock acquisition, WAL rewind conditions, synchronization tradeoffs, and remaining API edge cases; the number needed for saturation cannot be established.
